name: Mary Karungi: A Teacher's Rise to Educational Leadership

content.title: Mary Karungi: A Teacher's Rise to Educational Leadership
content.summary: An inspiring story of resilience learning and becoming an educational changemaker

media.caption: Karungi Mary: Empowering educators and redefining leadership through AKU's M.Ed programme
media.alt: Mary Karungi: A Teacher's Rise to Educational Leadership

content.text: For over 14 years, Karungi Mary taught with heart in Uganda, moving from classroom teacher to educator and mentor. She always knew that learning was the key to a better life, not just for her students, but for herself. Yet, even with her many degrees, including a Bachelor's and multiple Diplomas, she felt there was a bigger purpose calling her. She wanted to influence entire education systems, not just a single class.

In 2024, a lecturer at Kyambogo University introduced her to the Aga Khan University's Institute for Educational Development, East Africa (IED, EA). Mary was hooked by their global reputation and a style of learning that was hands-on and reflective. She enrolled full-time for her Master of Education in Tertiary Education, and that's where her journey truly began.
"I wanted to become a complete educator, one who influences not only classrooms but entire education systems," she recalls.

Studying at AKU was intense but incredibly rewarding. She found herself surrounded by people who pushed her to think deeper. The faculty didn't just teach; they mentored, strengthening her confidence as a leader. The assignments weren't just academic; they were about real-world problem-solving. "Their wisdom and encouragement strengthened my confidence as both an educator and a leader."

A major moment came during her practicum in Tanzania. Mary, a primary education expert, was placed in a secondary school - a surprise! Instead of waiting for a lesson plan, she saw an opportunity. Drawing on the critical thinking she learned at AKU, she led a mini-research project to help teachers adopt inclusive classroom practices. Through workshops and peer supervision, she and her team created a full research report in just five weeks. This challenge proved to her that teaching is a powerful tool for actual change.

Mary's personal life was tough. She was a widow and the sole provider for seven dependents, including her two orphaned children. To make ends meet while studying abroad, she tutored online and even learned hairdressing. Her resilience was noticed. During a practicum presentation, Professor Nicholas Wachira encouraged her to use her powerful, captivating voice beyond the classroom. "I realized my voice is not just my teaching tool," she says. "It's my platform for impact."

Today, Mary is no longer just a teacher. She facilitates professional development, mentors fellow educators, and works as a research assistant. She's looking ahead to a PhD and plans to establish a vocational institution to empower women and youth.
Her message is simple: "Go for it. AKU is more than a university; it's a life-changing community. It challenges you to ask not just 'What can I teach?' but 'What more can I do beyond teaching?'"
She adds: "I joined as a teacher, but I am graduating as an educational leader, researcher, and change-maker ready to serve my community and the world."
